faq.heading: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Can I encode and decode files, not just text?
faq.a1: Yes. In Text → Decode, recognized images appear directly in Output with a download button; binary data that cannot be read as text can also be downloaded there. Use Files & images to encode a local file or set the decoded file name and MIME type.
faq.a2: Yes — toggle URL-safe encoding for use in URLs or filenames.
faq.q3: Can it preview image files after decoding?
faq.a3: Recognized PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP, ICO and AVIF bytes are detected automatically, including raw Base64 without a data URI. A preview and download appear in Output. Browser support determines whether an image format can be displayed. This automatic file preview is not used in line-by-line mode.

article.heading: What is Base64, and why encode something in the first place?
article.p1: Base64 turns arbitrary binary data — an image, a PDF, a chunk of encrypted bytes — into a string made up only of the 64 characters A–Z, a–z, 0–9, +, and / (plus = for padding). It isn't encryption or compression; a Base64 string is roughly 33% larger than the data it represents, and anyone can decode it back instantly with no key required. The reason it exists is much more mundane: a lot of transport formats and storage systems — email (MIME attachments), JSON fields, URL query parameters, CSS/HTML `data:` URIs, config files — were built to carry plain text safely, and choke on raw binary bytes like line-feed characters or embedded nulls. Base64-encoding a binary payload turns it into a chunk of plain text that any of those systems can carry without corrupting it.
article.p2: This tool runs the encoding and decoding with plain JavaScript directly in your browser — nothing you type or upload is sent to a server. Text is encoded using `TextEncoder`/`btoa` under the hood so multi-byte UTF-8 characters (emoji, accented letters, CJK text) round-trip correctly, not just plain ASCII. Files are read locally via the browser's `FileReader` API, which means a multi-megabyte image never leaves your machine just to find out what its Base64 form looks like.
article.p3: For the usual workflow, paste your data in Text and select Encode or Decode; the result updates as you type. In Decode, recognized image bytes show a preview, MIME type, size and download button directly in Output, without switching tabs. Binary bytes that cannot be decoded as text can be downloaded as a file. Plain text still appears as text. Line by line processes separate values rather than one image. Files & images reads a local file to produce both raw Base64 and a data URI, and provides controls for the decoded MIME type and file name. URL-safe encoding replaces + and / with - and _ for use in URLs. Encoding is local; the original file is never uploaded.
article.p4: A common point of confusion worth flagging directly: Base64 is an encoding, not a security measure. A Base64 string is trivially reversible by design, so it should never be used as a substitute for real encryption — if you're looking to protect a token or a secret, encode it for transport with this tool by all means, but don't mistake that for hiding it. For inspecting the structure of an already-decoded JSON payload, the JSON Formatter & Validator tool is a natural next stop.
